newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Lufthansa defies strike threat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lufthansa defies strike threat.

text.p: German airline Lufthansa AG on Wednesday ignored the growing threat of strikes among its 50,000-plus workforce by announcing a plan to cut at least 10 percent of its core management and administration staff.

The news came as the DAG trade union, currently balloting staff on industrial action in a lengthy pay dispute, said it was increasingly confident of securing the necessary 70 percent agreement among its members for all-out strikes to go ahead.

Union officials said the move, which comes only days after Lufthansa chairman Juergen Weber promised in a personal letter to staff that its aim was to create more jobs in Germany, would be seen as a "declaration of war" by many of the employees.

But shares in the German national carrier surged almost six percent on the news as analysts welcomed the streamlining as a necessary step ahead of the full liberalisation of the European aviation market this year.
Weber, who was scheduled as a guest speaker at a conference on the airline industry in Frankfurt, defended the move in terms of the increased competition expected as a result of liberalisation.
"The pressure on costs that comes from open markets has meant airlines must take new positions in which many questions have to be asked," Weber told the conference.
"In liberalised markets, only those competitors with the lowest costs can take the strategic options needed to secure their existence," he added.

Lufthansa, due to be fully privatised at the end of the year, had earlier said in a statement it would group all its passenger services in a separate division which will act as a profit centre with its own management board.

The move marks the completion of a restructuring begun in 1994 and takes effect on April 1, coinciding with the implementation of an open skies agreement which will allow airlines to compete for all routes in Europe.
The airline said it would be creating a wide-ranging passenger division under which sales, marketing, network management, flight and staff operations would be brought together.

Lufthansa said the new measures would in themselves lead to the loss of only around 100 management and administration positions within its core scheduled business and costs related to the move are already provisioned for in the 1996 accounts.

But Michael Tarp, chief negotiator of the DAG union, said he feared the reorganisation would allow the airline eventually to spin out its operations into legally-separate divisions, thus allowing it to renegotiate cheaper worker contracts.
"In that sense it looks as if our worst expectations could be exceeded," Tarp said by telephone.

Tarp said that ballot documents received so far indicated that it would exceed the threshold of 70 percent of its members required in favour of a strike when the votes are counted it from February 25.

Limited industrial action carried out so far has already cost Lufthansa tens of millions of marks in lost business. DAG has rejected wage offers made by the airline so far as insufficient and below the industry average.

The rising threat of strikes was brushed off by the Frankfurt stock exchange as airline analysts gave a cautious welcome to the changes, noting however that the savings were likely to be relatively small.

"It makes sense if responsibility for costs and earnings is placed with a new layer of management and it makes sense to combine activities which belong together under one management," said Uwe Weinreich, aviation analyst at BHF-BANK.
Shares in the airline ended bourse trade 1.23 marks higher at 23.38, just off a day's high of 23.50.
But analysts noted that Lufthansa's shares could soon once again come under pressure when it publishes what are widely expected to be weaker earnings for 1996.
And when the skies open in April, Lufthansa will be confronted with competitors like British Airways and KLM which have worked just as hard to cut costs, they said.
